summary:
A trans visitor to Idaho stands under the United States federal framework in every respect concerning documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening that matches one's presentation.

Within Idaho, facility use is criminalised. House Bill 752, signed by the governor and effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match their birth sex in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. The first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail; a repeat offence within five years carries a felony of up to five years.

Contested status is the practical reality rather than settled law. On 30 April 2026 the ACLU of Idaho filed suit arguing that HB 752 violates due process, equal protection and privacy and targets no actual criminal conduct; six transgender Idahoans brought the challenge before the law's 1 July 2026 effect. The ACLU describes the measure as the only state law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses and as carrying steeper penalties than other states' bans. National wire reporting on the legislature's passage of the ban and the jail threats it carries states that the lawsuit has partially blocked it.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.
tangentialFactors:
Idaho's facility law sits inside a wider pattern. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Enforcement has already produced an arrest. In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents are the other fast-moving restriction. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, with rights groups describing the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
localsOnly:
Four successive legislative rounds ran in Idaho from 2023 to 2026, culminating in HB 752; the law reaches residents and visitors alike, since liability turns on birth sex rather than on documents presented or residency status.

Facility liability attaches in settings residents use routinely: government buildings and public-facing private businesses, with the enumerations covering gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A second qualifying offence within five years is charged as a felony carrying up to five years, so a resident's exposure escalates on repetition rather than on the seriousness of any underlying conduct, which the ACLU's filing states the law does not address.

The constitutional challenge was brought by six transgender Idahoans alongside the ACLU's 30 April 2026 filing, and rests on due-process, equal-protection and privacy grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope and durability of any injunction against HB 752 are not resolved in the sources available here: national wire reporting states the lawsuit partially blocked the law, but the provisions stayed, the dates involved and the current operative status of the 1 July 2026 effective date are not sourced.

Whether a trans resident or visitor can alter the sex marker on an Idaho birth certificate or driver's licence is not sourced in this inventory; the Movement Advancement Project map is referenced as the state-by-state authority but Idaho's specific conditions are not stated here.

The outcome of the ACLU of Idaho's constitutional challenge, and any appellate or Supreme Court review of it, is not sourced.

The identity of the 13 July 2026 national legal risk assessment and the criteria by which Idaho and the other three states were designated do-not-travel are not stated in the inventory.
